content.p: On 28 December 1962, military and police units moved into Palma Sola, a rural settlement in the San Juan province, in the southwest of República Dominicana. The settlement had grown into the centre of a religious movement that followed the teachings of Olivorio Mateo, a healer known as Papá Liborio. By the end of the day a general sent to clear the settlement was dead, dozens of followers lay dead in the hills and around the houses, and hundreds more had been taken prisoner. Nobody has agreed on the number of dead since.

The operation came eight days after Juan Bosch's party won the national election of 20 December 1962, while the country was still governed by a Consejo de Estado that governed in the period after the fall of the dictator Rafael Leónidas Trujillo. A 2026 commentary in Acento argues that the state wanted to break the movement up before the new government took office, which was due to happen on 27 February 1963. That is the commentator's reading, not a finding of any inquiry.
content.h2: A movement that outlived its founder
content.p: Olivorio Mateo was born in 1876 in San Juan de la Maguana. He lived as a farmer until 1908, when he disappeared for several days. When he came back, he said he had received a divine mission, and he began preaching prayer, farm work, mutual help and care for the poor. His following grew into thousands of people. The movement mixed folk healing with practices from several churches, and a strong sense of national pride with calls for social justice.

When forces from Estados Unidos occupied República Dominicana from 1916 to 1924, the movement became a focus of resistance in the eyes of the occupiers. Mateo was killed by occupation troops on 27 June 1922. His followers kept their faith hidden through the occupation and then through the Trujillo dictatorship, which had also persecuted the movement. The historian Roberto Cassá, who directed the Archivo General de la Nación, later described the movement after 1922 as a social response to a weak state, and argued that its followers came to want a worldly power that the original teaching had never sought.
content.h2: The revival under the Ventura brothers
content.p: After Trujillo was assassinated on 30 May 1961, the movement came back into the open. Its followers adopted the name Unión Cristiana Mundial. Its leaders were twin brothers, León Romilio and Plinio Ventura Rodríguez, who were known as Los Mellizos de Palma Sola. They established a community at Palma Sola, where the followers built a church and three calvaries, and where new members took oaths and undertook acts of sacrifice in the hope of forgiveness. Acento says that the brothers were believed by many to have the spirit of Liborio in them, and that people came from nearby towns to live close to them.

One follower, César Enrique Cuevas, told El Caribe in 1962 that he had registered about 10,000 believers. Another, a farmer named Policarpio Vicente, told the local authorities that about 5,000 men were drilling in groups of fifty, and that a corporal had a revolver brought from Haití. A confidential report held by the authorities also said that more weapons were expected from Haití. These claims came from people with an interest in the story, and the pages opened do not test them.
content.h2: The press campaign and the ultimatum
content.p: In the months before the killings, the movement was attacked in the press. Accounts from the time say that businesses, professional bodies, churches of several denominations and other groups in San Juan de la Maguana protested to the national and local governments. The complaints described sexual immorality, sorcery, animal sacrifice and the supposed endangering of public peace. Lucitania Martínez, a sociologist and philosopher who wrote a study of the community, reports that the complainants wanted a swift response from the government.

A report in the newspaper La Nación on 2 December 1962, cited by El Día and by Martínez, said that the complainants had set a deadline of 12 December for the government to act, and that otherwise the population would take matters into its own hands. Some reports also said that the followers were supporters of Trujillo. The brothers denied this in later interviews, and the pages opened give no evidence for it.

The official version, as recorded by the writer John Bartlow Martin in his account of the period and summarised by Acento, said that General Miguel Rodríguez Reyes went to Palma Sola to speak with the brothers. According to that version, hundreds of men came out of the huts and beat him to death with sticks. The police then used tear gas and opened fire. Three officers were wounded, and the police killed between 20 and 25 followers, among them two of the Ventura brothers. Some 673 prisoners were taken, and the settlement was set on fire.

El Caribe later spoke to two detained men, Medardo Céspedes and Gerardo Cuevas Agramonte. They said that the general was stabbed in the back of the neck and then beaten with sticks, and that the attack began after a police officer asked a man in the crowd to hand over a knife. Cuevas named the Ventura brothers as responsible for the confrontation. Both men were prisoners when they spoke, and the paper reported their words without independent confirmation.

Martin's account also records that about 500 people fled into the mountains. Acento reports that they were pursued by two counter-insurgency companies and by P-51 aircraft that strafed them from the air. The same account records that, on the night before the operation, the chief of the military advisory group was asked to provide helicopters, ammunition and 60 tanks of napalm for the P-51 aircraft. The pages opened do not confirm that napalm was used.

The number of dead is the hardest question. El Caribe, reporting in the days after the killings, counted 42 bodies and said that more than 42 people died; the same newspaper also described more than thirty bodies scattered across the area. CDN reports that the official figure at the time was 42, that other estimates ran above 100, and that some put the figure close to 800. It says that the dead, including women and children, were buried in common graves. El Caribe, in contrast, reported that the bodies were cremated.

In 2012 the director of the Archivo General de la Nación, Roberto Cassá, told a conference marking the 50th anniversary that the count was higher than the official figure, and he put it at 200 bloody deaths. A commentary in Acento in 2026 said that the exact number of bodies remains unknown. The pages opened do not establish a single figure, so no single figure is given here.

General Rodríguez Reyes had served under Trujillo. El Día reports that Bosch had assured him the post of minister of the armed forces, and that neither the advisers from Estados Unidos nor the conservative Unión Cívica Nacional favoured him. The newspapers' public explanation for the operation was his death, and the commentary in El Día argues that the accusation against the brothers was a political move by a conservative group. That is the view of the writer, not an established finding.
The reports also disagree on his first name. El Día gives Miguel F. Rodríguez Reyes, while El Caribe gives Manuel F. Rodríguez Reyes. Both agree on his surname and that he was killed.

Acento's account of the officials from Estados Unidos who went with the troops says that the president of the Consejo de Estado, Rafael F. Bonnelly, was deeply affected by the general's death and was convinced that the followers had weapons. He reportedly told the officials that the military planned to destroy the other camps and to scatter the prisoners around the country. He also agreed that Estados Unidos should stay out of the matter.

Francisco Alberto Caamaño Deñó, who led the troops under the general, was wounded in the operation. CDN says he later became a national hero. The pages opened do not describe any trial of the people held after the killings. CDN writes that no government has chosen to open this chapter of the record into a proper inquiry.

León Romilio Ventura Rodríguez survived the operation. He was detained and taken to the prison in San Juan de la Maguana in mid-December 1962, and El Caribe later reported that he was the only one of the five Ventura brothers to survive. In a later interview he denied that the movement supported Trujillo. He said the dictatorship had killed his ancestors and scattered his family.

The Archivo General de la Nación marked the 50th anniversary in December 2012 with talks, and historians planned to go to the province on 27 and 28 December to hold discussions there. Acento's commentary in 2026 described the massacre as one of the most silenced episodes in the country's history.

Several questions remain open. The first is the death toll, which runs from 20 to 25 in the official version recorded by Martin to 800 in the highest estimate. The second is the fate of the Ventura brothers. The official version says police killed two of them, while El Caribe's reports name four brothers, Eloy, Plinio, Tulio and Nicolás, among the dead. The third is what happened to the bodies. The fourth is whether napalm was used.

Testimony from the day itself comes from detained men, from official accounts recorded later, and from newspapers of the time. The date, 28 December, is the Día de los Santos Inocentes. Acento says there is no conclusive evidence that the operation was timed for that date, but notes the irony. The pages opened do not show who gave the final order, and no investigation has been found that answers the question.
